nodes.title: Storage concepts: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

questions.q: An administrator is configuring a new database server and needs to combine four 2 TB drives into a single fault-tolerant volume that survives one drive failure while still providing a usable capacity larger than 4 TB. Which RAID level BEST meets these requirements?
choices: RAID 5 — distributed parity across all members, tolerates one drive failure, usable capacity equals (n−1) × drive size
RAID 0 — data striped across all drives with no parity, providing maximum capacity and performance
RAID 1 — data mirrored between drive pairs, tolerates one failure per mirror but halves usable capacity
RAID 6 — dual distributed parity, tolerates two drive failures but reduces usable capacity by two drives
questions.explanation: RAID 5 uses one drive's worth of distributed parity, so four 2 TB drives yield 6 TB of usable capacity (above the 4 TB target) and survive a single drive failure. RAID 0 has no fault tolerance — any drive loss destroys the array. RAID 1 mirrors pairs and would only deliver 4 TB total, not exceeding the 4 TB requirement. RAID 6 survives two failures but only delivers 4 TB usable capacity from this set, failing the >4 TB requirement.

questions.q: A company wants to consolidate ten physical servers onto two large hosts and needs the lowest virtualization overhead and direct access to the underlying CPU, memory and I/O. Which hypervisor architecture should they deploy?
choices: A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor such as VMware Workstation or Oracle VirtualBox installed on top of Windows or Linux
A containerized runtime such as Docker that shares the host kernel rather than virtualizing hardware
A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor such as VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V Server, or Citrix Hypervisor installed directly on the server hardware
A nested virtualization stack with Type 2 hypervisors layered inside guest virtual machines
questions.explanation: Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors run directly on the hardware and present virtual hardware to guests without an intervening host OS, giving the lowest overhead and the most direct access to CPU, memory, and I/O resources — exactly what production server consolidation requires. Type 2 hypervisors run as applications on a general-purpose OS and incur extra context-switching overhead. Containers share the host kernel and do not virtualize hardware (they virtualize the OS), so they do not satisfy the requirement to abstract physical hardware. Nested virtualization adds layers, increasing overhead rather than reducing it.

questions.q: A data center needs to deploy 32 compute nodes in the smallest possible footprint while sharing power supplies, cooling fans, and management modules across the group. Which server form factor BEST fits this requirement?
choices: Tower servers installed in a row on an open shelving unit for maximum airflow
Blade servers installed in a shared chassis that provides common power, cooling, and management
Standard 1U rack-mount servers cabled individually into a 42U rack
Mainframe-class systems partitioned into LPARs and accessed remotely
questions.explanation: Blade servers are designed exactly for this scenario: a chassis (also called an enclosure) hosts multiple blade modules that share PSUs, cooling fans, and management/network fabric, achieving the highest server-per-U density. Tower servers are floor-standing units used for low-density branch deployments and waste rack space. Standard 1U rack servers each carry their own PSUs and fans and consume one full rack unit per node, so 32 nodes would fill most of a rack. Mainframes are large, expensive single systems, not a way to consolidate many independent servers in a compact footprint.

questions.q: An administrator must present raw, block-level storage to a virtualization cluster so that each host treats the volumes as if they were local SCSI disks. Which storage architecture meets this requirement?
choices: Direct-attached storage (DAS) using internal SATA disks inside each host
Object storage accessed via an HTTP REST API such as S3-compatible endpoints
Network-attached storage (NAS) exporting volumes via NFS or SMB file shares
Storage area network (SAN) using Fibre Channel or iSCSI to present LUNs as block devices
questions.explanation: A SAN delivers block-level storage over a dedicated fabric (Fibre Channel) or over IP (iSCSI/FCoE), and each LUN appears to the host as a local SCSI disk — the model hypervisors expect for shared datastores and clustered file systems. NAS presents files over NFS/SMB, not raw blocks. Object storage exposes opaque objects through REST APIs, not block devices. DAS provides block storage but only to the single host it's plugged into, so it cannot be shared across a cluster.

questions.q: A finance database server is experiencing intermittent crashes that logs trace to single-bit memory errors. The company wants memory that can detect and silently correct these errors without crashing the OS. Which memory technology should be specified for the replacement DIMMs?
choices: Registered (RDIMM) memory with on-DIMM buffering but no parity checking
ECC (error-correcting code) memory that detects and corrects single-bit errors and detects multi-bit errors
Unbuffered non-ECC DDR4 memory with the highest available clock speed
Load-reduced DIMM (LRDIMM) memory configured in dual-rank mode
questions.explanation: ECC memory adds an extra chip and uses Hamming-code parity to detect AND silently correct single-bit errors and detect (but not correct) most multi-bit errors — the precise behavior needed for finance and database workloads where data integrity matters. RDIMM and LRDIMM refer to electrical buffering for capacity/stability, not error correction; they may or may not include ECC. Non-ECC memory does not detect bit flips at all, so silent corruption can occur.

questions.q: A business-continuity plan states that after an outage the order-processing system can lose at most 15 minutes of data and must be back online within 1 hour. Which terms correctly describe these two thresholds?
choices: RPO is 15 minutes (maximum tolerable data loss) and RTO is 1 hour (maximum tolerable downtime)
RTO is 15 minutes (maximum tolerable data loss) and RPO is 1 hour (maximum tolerable downtime)
MTBF is 15 minutes and MTTR is 1 hour — both are measured backward from the point of failure
SLA is 15 minutes and SLO is 1 hour — these are contractual penalties for missed targets
questions.explanation: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time — the gap between the last good backup/replica and the failure. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable downtime — how long the service may remain unavailable. The other option swaps the two definitions. MTBF (mean time between failures) and MTTR (mean time to repair) are reliability metrics, not recovery targets. SLAs and SLOs are agreements/objectives covering broader service quality and do not specifically map to these recovery thresholds.

questions.q: A backup policy runs a full backup every Sunday and a different backup every other night. The administrator wants each weeknight job to copy only the files that have changed since the most recent backup of ANY type, minimizing nightly backup size and time. Which backup type satisfies this requirement?
choices: Differential backup — copies everything changed since the last full backup, growing each night until the next full
Synthetic full backup — reconstructs a full backup on the backup server without re-reading client data
Incremental backup — copies only the files changed since the most recent backup of any type, then clears the archive bit
Mirror backup — maintains an exact one-to-one copy of source data with no historical versions retained
questions.explanation: An incremental backup copies only files changed since the most recent backup of any type (full or incremental) and clears the archive bit, producing the smallest nightly job. A differential backup copies everything changed since the last FULL backup, so its size grows every night until the next full. A synthetic full is built from existing backups on the backup server — it does not reduce client-side backup windows on weeknights. A mirror backup keeps an exact copy with no versioning, so it cannot satisfy a rotated weekly/nightly policy.

questions.q: On an iSCSI SAN, an administrator is mapping a new LUN to a server. Which statement correctly describes the roles of the iSCSI initiator and the iSCSI target?
choices: The initiator runs on the storage array and pushes data to passive targets running on each application server
Initiator and target are interchangeable peers — either side can mount LUNs presented by the other
The target is a Fibre Channel concept that does not apply to iSCSI deployments over Ethernet
The initiator runs on the host (server) and the target runs on the storage array — the host's initiator logs in to the array's target to access LUNs
questions.explanation: In iSCSI, the initiator is the client component on the host that issues SCSI commands, and the target is the service on the storage array that exposes one or more LUNs. The host's initiator (software or HBA) authenticates and logs in to the array's target portal to discover and mount the LUNs. The roles are NOT symmetric, and "target" is standard iSCSI terminology (not Fibre Channel-only). The storage array does not push data to passive clients; the initiator pulls/pushes blocks through standard SCSI request/response.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.
Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.
Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: A critical server is installed with dual hot-swappable power supplies. To realize the full availability benefit of the redundant PSUs, how should the supplies be connected?
choices: Connect each PSU to a different power circuit/PDU, ideally fed from independent UPSs, so a single circuit or UPS failure does not down the server
Connect both PSUs to the same UPS-protected outlet to guarantee identical voltage and phase to each supply
Connect one PSU to utility power and leave the second unplugged as a cold spare to extend its service life
Connect both PSUs to the rack PDU but disable the second supply in the BIOS until the first fails
questions.explanation: Dual PSUs only protect against power-path failures if each one is fed from an independent circuit and ideally an independent UPS. That way, loss of one circuit, breaker, or UPS still leaves the server powered. Plugging both into the same outlet, leaving the second unplugged, or disabling it in BIOS all collapse the redundancy back to a single point of failure, defeating the purpose of the second PSU.

questions.q: An administrator is hardening a newly installed Windows Server. Which action follows the principle of reducing the server's attack surface MOST directly?
choices: Open every non-privileged TCP port so that legitimate clients never see a connection refused message
Disable all unused services, close unneeded network ports, and remove or rename default administrative accounts
Grant the Administrators group access to every share so that troubleshooting tickets can be resolved quickly
Disable Windows Defender and the host firewall to avoid performance interference with line-of-business apps
questions.explanation: Reducing attack surface means turning off anything not strictly needed: stop and disable unused services, block unused ports at the host firewall, and remove or rename default accounts to eliminate well-known credentials. Opening every port, granting blanket administrator access, or disabling the antivirus and firewall would all enlarge the attack surface and weaken host security rather than harden it.

questions.q: After replacing a server's motherboard, the administrator wants to ensure the system will only execute boot loaders and firmware signed by trusted authorities, preventing pre-OS rootkits. Which UEFI feature should be enabled?
choices: Legacy/CSM boot mode so that older signed bootloaders can still load via the BIOS interface
Hyper-Threading (SMT) and Intel VT-x, which together gate which boot images the firmware will accept
Secure Boot — UEFI verifies the cryptographic signature of bootloaders and firmware against the platform's signature database before executing them
Wake-on-LAN with magic-packet authentication so the server only powers on for authorized administrators
questions.explanation: UEFI Secure Boot maintains a signature database (db) and a forbidden database (dbx) and refuses to execute any bootloader or driver whose signature is not in db or whose hash appears in dbx — exactly the protection against pre-OS bootkits/rootkits the question describes. Legacy/CSM mode deliberately bypasses Secure Boot. SMT and VT-x are CPU features unrelated to boot validation. Wake-on-LAN controls remote power-up, not what code is allowed to execute at boot.

questions.q: A data center is suffering from hot spots in the racks and rising cooling costs. The facilities team proposes a hot-aisle / cold-aisle containment layout. What is the PRIMARY cooling benefit of this arrangement?
choices: It allows every server to face the same direction so cabling can be standardized across the data center
It eliminates the need for raised floors by venting hot exhaust directly into the rack overheads
It guarantees the CRAC units can be turned off during cold weather without raising intake temperatures
It separates server exhaust (hot aisle) from server intake (cold aisle), preventing recirculation of hot air into intakes and improving CRAC efficiency
questions.explanation: Hot-aisle / cold-aisle layouts orient racks so that intakes face one shared aisle (cold) and exhausts face the opposite aisle (hot), and containment seals one aisle so the two air masses do not mix. That prevents hot exhaust from recirculating into server intakes, lowers the supply-air temperature required from the CRAC/CRAH units, and significantly improves cooling efficiency (better PUE). The arrangement is about airflow separation — not about cabling, eliminating raised floors, or letting CRAC units be turned off entirely.

questions.q: A server has four identical disks. The business needs the fault tolerance to survive ANY two simultaneous disk failures while still using the array for data. Which RAID level meets this with these four disks?
choices: RAID 5, which uses single distributed parity across all four disks
RAID 6, which uses dual distributed parity and tolerates two disk failures
RAID 0, which stripes the data evenly across all four disks for the maximum possible read and write performance
RAID 1, mirroring the four disks into two independent mirrored pairs
questions.explanation: RAID 6 keeps two independent parity blocks distributed across the set, so any two drives can fail without data loss — exactly the requirement (and four disks is the practical minimum). RAID 5 survives only one failure; RAID 0 has no redundancy; RAID 1 mirrored pairs survive two failures only if they're in different pairs, not 'any two', so it doesn't guarantee the requirement.

questions.q: After a power event, a server with a hardware RAID 5 array reports the array is 'degraded' but still online. A replacement disk has been inserted. What is happening when the controller begins 'rebuilding'?
choices: The controller reconstructs the missing disk's data onto the replacement using parity and the surviving disks
The controller reformats every disk in the array from scratch and restores all data from the most recent verified backup set
The array converts itself to RAID 6 automatically to prevent a future second failure
The controller mirrors the newest surviving disk byte-for-byte onto the replacement disk
questions.explanation: A degraded RAID 5 is running on its surviving members; inserting a replacement triggers a rebuild that recomputes the lost drive's contents from the remaining data and parity and writes it to the new disk — no backup or reformat involved. RAID levels don't self-convert, and parity reconstruction is not a simple byte-for-byte mirror of one disk.

questions.q: A technician must justify to management why production servers run ECC memory while desktops do not. What is ECC's primary benefit?
choices: It increases total addressable memory capacity beyond what non-ECC modules allow
It detects and corrects single-bit memory errors, preventing silent data corruption and crashes
It runs at substantially higher memory clock speeds, improving overall throughput for demanding server applications
It encrypts the contents of RAM so memory-scraping attacks cannot read sensitive data
questions.explanation: Error-Correcting Code memory uses extra bits to detect and correct single-bit errors (and detect multi-bit), preventing the silent corruption and crashes that matter on always-on servers handling critical data. ECC doesn't raise capacity or clock speed (it's marginally slower) and provides no encryption of memory contents.

questions.q: A backup policy runs a full backup Sunday and INCREMENTAL backups Monday through Saturday. A failure occurs Thursday afternoon. Which backup sets are needed to fully restore?
choices: Sunday's full plus Thursday's incremental only, since each incremental is self-contained
Thursday's incremental only, because incrementals always include all prior changes
Sunday's full plus every incremental from Monday through Wednesday in order
Sunday's full plus Wednesday's incremental, the most recent complete daily set
questions.explanation: An incremental captures only what changed since the LAST backup of any type, so restoration requires the last full plus each incremental in sequence up to the failure: Sunday full + Monday + Tuesday + Wednesday (Thursday's may be incomplete). Differentials would need only the full plus the latest one — that's the distinction the exam tests.

nodes.title: Troubleshooting methodology: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

questions.q: A disaster recovery plan specifies an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 4 hours for an order database. What do these two values constrain, respectively?
choices: RPO sets the maximum acceptable data loss; RTO sets the maximum acceptable time to restore service
RPO sets how long restoration may take; RTO sets how much data may be lost in the gap
Both define backup frequency, with RPO for full backups and RTO for incrementals
RPO is the retention period for which backup copies are kept; RTO is the rotation interval at which the tape media is cycled offsite
questions.explanation: Recovery Point Objective is how far back the recovery point may be — i.e. the maximum tolerable data loss (15 minutes of transactions); Recovery Time Objective is how long the business can be down before service is restored (4 hours). Confusing the two is the classic trap; neither defines retention or media rotation.

questions.q: Two servers must share access to the same block storage LUNs on a Fibre Channel SAN, and the storage admin needs to control exactly which initiators can see which LUNs. Which two SAN techniques enforce this isolation?
choices: VLAN tagging on the SAN switches and ACLs on each server's iSCSI initiator
Zoning on the fabric switches and LUN masking on the storage array
Subnetting the storage network and applying NTFS permissions on each LUN
Link aggregation across the HBAs and share-level permissions on the volumes
questions.explanation: Zoning at the FC fabric switch level controls which initiators and targets can communicate, and LUN masking at the array controls which hosts a given LUN is presented to — the two complementary access controls for SAN storage. VLANs/subnets and NTFS/share permissions operate at the IP-network and filesystem layers, not FC block presentation.

questions.q: A technician hardening a new server applies the principle of least functionality. Which action best reflects this principle?
choices: Installing every available role and feature so the server can handle any future need
Disabling or removing unneeded services, roles, ports and default accounts to shrink the attack surface
Granting all of the server's administrators full local Administrator rights up front to maximize day-to-day operational flexibility
Leaving default vendor credentials in place but documenting them in the runbook
questions.explanation: Least functionality means a system should provide only the capabilities required for its purpose — disable/remove unneeded services, roles, ports, software and default accounts to minimize the attack surface. Installing everything, broad admin rights, and retained default credentials all enlarge the attack surface, the opposite of the principle.

questions.q: Servers in a rack are overheating. The data center uses a hot-aisle/cold-aisle layout. Which practice MOST directly preserves the effectiveness of that layout?
choices: Installing blanking panels in empty rack U spaces to stop hot and cold air mixing
Raising the room's overall thermostat set point to reduce total cooling energy use
Orienting alternating servers to face opposite directions to balance the airflow
Bundling all power and network cables tightly across the rear of the rack openings
questions.explanation: Blanking (filler) panels in unused U spaces prevent hot exhaust air from recirculating to the cold intake side through the open gaps — preserving aisle separation and intake temperatures. Raising the set point worsens it; servers must all draw from the cold aisle (consistent orientation), not alternate; and dense cabling over the rear blocks exhaust, hurting airflow.

questions.q: A server's dual hot-swap power supplies are both plugged into the same rack PDU. An electrician must service that PDU. What design change removes this single point of failure?
choices: Connecting each power supply to a separate PDU fed from an independent power circuit
Replacing both power supplies with a single higher-wattage redundant unit
Adding a third power supply to the same PDU for additional headroom
Scheduling the PDU maintenance work to occur during the application's regular nightly backup window so users are least affected
questions.explanation: Redundant power supplies only help if they're fed from independent sources — each PSU on a separate PDU and circuit (ideally with diverse upstream UPS/utility feeds) so losing one path keeps the server up. Sharing one PDU makes it the single point of failure; one combined PSU or a third PSU on the same PDU doesn't add path diversity; scheduling still causes an outage.

questions.q: Users report a server is reachable by its IP address but not by its hostname, while other servers resolve fine. Which is the MOST likely cause to investigate first?
choices: A missing or incorrect DNS A record (or stale cache) for that specific server's hostname
A failed network cable between the server and the access-layer switch port
An expired TLS certificate on the application the server is hosting for clients
Insufficient installed RAM that causes the server's local name-resolution service to crash and restart repeatedly under load
questions.explanation: Reachable by IP but not by name is a name-resolution problem: the server's A record is missing, wrong, or cached stale in clients/resolvers — that's the first thing to check. A failed cable would break IP connectivity too; an expired certificate produces TLS warnings, not name-resolution failure; the server is clearly up, so a crashing local service isn't indicated.
